candidate.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — modifiable CKD risk reduction
candidate.educational_objective: Reduce CKD risk through management of hypertension, diabetes, excess weight, and potentially nephrotoxic medication exposure while promoting appropriate early kidney screening in at-risk adults.

options.A: Work with the health care team to control blood pressure and diabetes, address excess weight, avoid prolonged NSAID overuse, and obtain recommended kidney screening because these factors can affect CKD risk.
options.B: Kidney-disease risk is determined almost entirely by inherited factors, so blood pressure, diabetes, weight, and medication use have little relevance.
options.C: Wait for swelling or reduced urine output before addressing risk factors because CKD prevention and screening are not useful before symptoms develop.
options.D: Continue frequent NSAID use without review because overuse of these medicines is not associated with kidney injury or CKD risk.

candidate.rationale: Current National Kidney Foundation guidance identifies diabetes and hypertension as the most common CKD risk factors and also lists obesity and prolonged overuse of NSAID pain medicines among important risks. Risk-reduction guidance includes managing blood pressure and blood glucose, maintaining a healthy weight and lifestyle, reviewing potentially kidney-harming medicines, and obtaining kidney testing when risk is elevated because CKD may be asymptomatic until advanced. Therefore, A is correct. B minimizes established modifiable or treatable risk factors, C delays prevention and early detection, and D dismisses a recognized medication-related kidney risk.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Directly supports hypertension, diabetes, obesity, and prolonged NSAID overuse as actionable CKD-risk considerations and supports prevention/early screening rather than waiting for symptoms.
